issues.issue: The execution date is incomplete on its face — "the Ist day of ___ 1999" leaves the month blank, so the date of making cannot be determined from the words. That is a mechanical defect that bears on when obligations attached.

The preamble dates the making of the Agreement in 1999, while Section 11 (Effective Date) states the Agreement is effective August 1, 1997; the two cannot both be read literally. A court would have to decide which date governs.

The Custodian's duties are given as a closed enumeration with no catch-all, leaving open whether anything not listed (e.g. monitoring the investment manager or the account's contents) is a duty at all; expressio unius cuts one way and "be responsible for the collection of all investment income" cuts the other. The reach of the list is exactly what two parties would fight about.

The ministerial, direction-driven duties here sit awkwardly against Section 21's indemnity for loss by "mysterious disappearance", which imposes liability untethered to any listed duty. A court could be asked whether Section 1 caps the Custodian's responsibilities.

Subsection (c)'s catch-all — "any other instruments that may be necessary or appropriate to carry out the custodianship duties and powers" — follows specific documents of transfer and conveyance, so its reach is uncertain; "ministerial and other non-discretionary duties" in (b) is likewise a boundary term. The general-vs-specific tension is nameable.
"[A] market value for the assets of the account" fixes neither a valuation source nor a method, but the obligation itself is plain. Only mild vagueness.

"[S]uch other reports as the Owners may reasonably request, including reports ... as may be necessary" stacks two open-ended standards with no benchmark. The scope of the reporting duty is not fixed by the words.

Compensation is set "in Schedule A attached to this Agreement", but no Schedule A appears in the instrument, and its amendment "from time to time by the parties" is not tied to Section 6(a)'s requirement of written agreement. A court would have to supply or reconcile the missing term.

"[O]ut-of-pocket expenses during the reasonable performance of the Custodian's duties" misplaces the modifier: it is unclear whether "reasonable" limits the expenses or merely describes the performance. That misplacement changes what the Owner must reimburse.
The only defect is the typo "chenges"/"conceming", which does not alter meaning. The obligation to furnish and update the list is definite.

"[T]he oral advice as confirmed in writing or written advice of such persons" is syntactically ambiguous: it may mean the Custodian may act on oral advice only once confirmed in writing, or that written confirmation is merely one of two permitted forms. Whether reliance on unconfirmed oral instructions is protected turns on this reading.

Section 1(b)–(c) requires the Custodian to act and settle only on "written direction", which is difficult to square with any reading of this clause permitting reliance on oral advice. A court could be asked which controls.

Section 4 contemplates Schedule A being "amended from time to time by the parties" without any writing requirement, while this clause permits amendment only "by written agreement of the parties". The tension is mild but nameable.
"[U]nless or until terminated" is a clumsy conjunction, but the 30-day written-notice mechanic is plain. Nothing turns on the wording.

"[A]ll securities held in the account shall be delivered" on termination cannot be squared literally with Section 15, under which deposit securities are under the control of the Colorado Insurance Commissioner and may not be withdrawn without approval, nor with Section 6(d)'s withholding right. A court would have to harmonise them.
"[B]alances owing to the Custodian" is undefined and broader than "fees", leaving the extent of the withholding right uncertain. The clause also does not say how assets are valued when withheld.
This self-help right qualifies Section 6(c)'s unqualified command that "all securities held in the account shall be delivered" to the Owner. The two sentences pull against each other.

The carve-out turns on whether the Custodian "has committed negligence or malfeasance", terms that are neither defined nor allocated a decision-maker, and the indemnity's reach — whether it covers claims by the Owner itself as well as third parties — is not stated. Both are classic points of construction.

A broad Owner-indemnity for "any and all claims" the Custodian incurs by acting as Custodian is circular against Sections 21 and 22, which make the Custodian liable to the Owner for losses including no-fault "mysterious disappearance". Read together they can require the Owner to indemnify the Custodian against the very liability Section 21 creates.
"[R]elevant to this Agreement" is the only limit on an otherwise unbounded examination right, with no notice, place or procedure. The boundary of "relevant" is left to argument.

This unconditional inspection right conflicts with Section 17, which permits examination only during business hours, on the Custodian's premises, on reasonable notice and "only upon" written instructions from an appropriate officer of the Owner. Both cannot be applied literally.

The operative date is handwritten and garbled — "Aust { i 997" — so the effective date cannot be read off the instrument with confidence. A mechanical defect of this kind directly changes when the Agreement took effect.

The stated 1997 effective date cannot be reconciled with the preamble, which recites that the Agreement is made in 1999. A court asked when the custodial duties began would have to choose between them.

The Custodian is given a bare election — segregated holding "or" fungible bulk under a FOSBI arrangement — with no criteria and no notice obligation, and FOSBI is not defined. Which branch applies to any given security is not fixed by the text.
The clause permits four alternative registrations without saying who elects among them or on what basis. The permissive string leaves the Owner's protection dependent on an unallocated choice.

Registration "in the name of the Custodian or its nominee" sits in tension with Section 13, which requires the Custodian's records to identify the securities as "owned by the Owner", and with Section 15's withdrawal-on-demand right. The relationship of legal title to those rights is not spelled out.

"[T]o the extent required by those sections" makes the Commissioner's control depend on external statutes without identifying which securities are so "used to meet the deposit requirements". The boundary of the exception must be worked out from outside the document.

The absolute statement that custodied securities are "withdrawable upon the demand of the Owner" conflicts with Section 6(c)/(d), under which delivery on termination is subject to the Custodian's right to withhold for outstanding fees and balances. Both are stated in unqualified terms.

"[A]t such times and containing such information as may be reasonably requested" leaves the content and frequency of reporting entirely to an unbounded reasonableness standard. What a request may compel is not fixed.

This duplicates and overlaps Section 3's reporting obligations without saying which governs where they differ, leaving two reporting regimes in one instrument. The overlap is redundant rather than plainly contradictory.

"[A]ny representative of an appropriate regulatory body" and "an appropriate officer of the Owner" both turn on an undefined "appropriate", which decides who may compel access. The gatekeeping condition is therefore not self-applying.

The "but only upon furnishing ... written instructions" precondition cannot be squared with Section 9, which subjects the Custodian's books, records and practices to examination by the Owner with no conditions at all. A court would have to decide whether Section 17 qualifies Section 9.

The trailing qualifier "that the Owner may reasonably request" is ambiguous as to whether it limits only clause (b) or both (a) and (b), which decides whether clearing-corporation reports must be sent automatically. The syntax alone will not resolve it.

"[R]ecords sufficient to determine and verify information ... that may be reported in the Owner's Annual Statement" sets no ascertainable standard of sufficiency. What suffices is judged only after the fact.

"[M]ysterious disappearance" is a term of art with contested boundaries, and the clause mixes fault-based triggers (negligence, dishonesty) with no-fault ones (theft, mysterious disappearance, damage or destruction), so the standard of liability is not settled by the words. "[L]oss of custodied securities" is likewise undefined as against loss of value.

This liability cannot readily be reconciled with Section 7, under which the Owner indemnifies the Custodian for all claims incurred by acting as Custodian except where the Custodian was negligent or committed malfeasance — leaving no-fault losses indemnified in both directions. Section 23's force-majeure exculpation pulls the same way.

"[S]hall promptly replace the securities or the value thereof" does not say who elects between replacement in kind and payment, or as of what date value is fixed, and "the value of any loss of rights or privileges" is unquantified. The remedy is left unspecified in a clause whose whole purpose is remedy.

The exculpation ends in a catch-all — "or similar causes beyond its reasonable control" — appended to a long list of specific events, so ejusdem generis leaves its reach genuinely open; the list also contains the mechanical error "lot" for "riot". Whether an event is "similar" to war, strikes and acts of God is precisely what parties would dispute.

A blanket exculpation for "any failure to take any action required to be taken under the Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 21, which makes the Custodian liable for no-fault losses including theft and mysterious disappearance. A court would have to decide whether Section 23 cuts down Section 21.

The proviso lets "the Insurance Commissioner of the state of domicile of the insurance company" accept a different standard of liability, but the Agreement never defines "the insurance company" and gives no mechanism or timing for that acceptance. The clause's operation is left to an outside actor on undefined terms.

"[I]nsurance protection consistent with the requirements of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency" incorporates an unidentified external standard and fixes no amount, coverage or duration. Whether the warranty was met cannot be judged from the words alone.
